Example Online Services Safety Bill

Part 1: Definitions and scope

This Act applies to an online service that is accessible from within the jurisdiction and that allows users to create, share or view content generated by other users. A provider of such a service is called a platform operator in this Act. The Act does not apply to a service that is used only for internal communication within a single organisation, nor to a service operated by a public authority for the purpose of delivering a statutory function. The Minister may, by order, extend or narrow the scope of this Act after consulting the Regulator and publishing the reasons for the change.

In this Act, harmful content means content that the Regulator has designated, in a published code of practice, as likely to cause serious harm to a user or to the public. A designation must state the kind of content covered, the reasons for the designation and the date on which it takes effect. Before making a designation the Regulator must publish a draft, invite written comments for at least thirty days, and consider every comment received. A designation made without following that process has no effect, and the Regulator must say so on its website as soon as the defect is found.

A large platform is a platform operator whose service had more than one million active users in the jurisdiction during the previous calendar year. The Regulator must publish a list of large platforms each year and must update the list within fourteen days of learning that a platform has crossed the threshold. A platform operator that disagrees with its inclusion in the list may ask the Regulator to reconsider, giving evidence of its user numbers. The Regulator must reply in writing within thirty days and explain its decision, whether or not the operator’s request succeeds.

Part 2: Duties of platform operators

A platform operator must take reasonable steps to reduce the risk that users encounter harmful content on its service. What counts as reasonable depends on the size of the service, the likelihood and severity of the harm, and the cost and effectiveness of available measures. A platform operator must keep a written record of the steps it has taken and must give that record to the Regulator on request within fourteen days. The record must be kept for at least three years after the step it describes was last in use.

A large platform must also publish a transparency report twice a year. The report must set out the number of complaints received about harmful content, the number of items removed or restricted, the average time taken to act on a complaint, and the main reasons for any decision to leave reported content in place. The report must be written in plain language, be free to read, and be published in a form that allows the figures to be copied into a spreadsheet. A large platform must keep each report available on its website for at least five years.

Every platform operator must provide a simple way for users to report content and to appeal a decision about their own content. An operator must acknowledge a report within two working days and must tell the person who made the report what action was taken. If an operator removes a user’s content, it must tell that user which rule was breached and how to appeal. An appeal must be decided by a person who was not involved in the original decision, and the outcome must be explained in writing.

Part 3: Enforcement and review

The Regulator may require a platform operator to provide information that the Regulator reasonably needs to carry out its functions under this Act. A notice requiring information must state its purpose, the date by which the information is due and the consequences of not complying. A platform operator may ask the Regulator to extend the date where there is a good reason, such as the volume of material requested. The Regulator must not use information obtained under this section for any purpose other than the administration of this Act.

Where the Regulator finds that a platform operator has failed to comply with a duty under this Act, it may issue a compliance notice that sets out the failure, the steps required to remedy it and the period allowed. If the operator does not comply with the notice, the Regulator may impose a financial penalty. The penalty must be proportionate, must take account of the size of the operator and the seriousness of the failure, and must not exceed the amount set out in the schedule. An operator may appeal a penalty to the High Court within thirty days.

The Minister must arrange for an independent review of this Act within three years of the day it comes into force. The reviewer must consult platform operators, users, civil society groups and the Regulator, and must report to the Minister in writing. The Minister must lay the report before Parliament within three months of receiving it, together with a statement of whether the Government accepts the reviewer’s recommendations and, if not, why not. Nothing in this section prevents an earlier review if the Minister considers one to be necessary.
